[Object] plays a central role in [area]. The study of [object] goes back to [author], who showed that [result]. A basic question in [area] is whether [question]. Over the last decade, [object] has attracted considerable attention because [reason]. Despite this progress, little is known about [gap].
Stating the problem and the gap

The main difficulty is that [obstacle]. Existing methods do not apply when [condition]. To our knowledge, the case [case] has not been treated. This leaves open the question of whether [question]. The purpose of this paper is to [aim].

Our main result is the following. We prove that [statement]. We show that [statement] holds under the weaker assumption [assumption]. As a consequence, we obtain [corollary]. In particular, this answers a question of [author]. This extends a result of [author] from [setting A] to [setting B].

The proof relies on [technique]. The key idea is to [idea]. We proceed in three steps. First, [step one]. Then, [step two]. Finally, [step three]. Our approach differs from [earlier approach] in that [difference]. The main new ingredient is [ingredient].

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls the necessary background on [topic]. In Section 3 we prove [result]. Section 4 contains examples and applications. We conclude with open questions in Section 5.

Throughout the paper, [convention]. We say that [object] is [property] if [condition]. Recall that [definition]. We write [notation] for [meaning]. Unless stated otherwise, all [objects] are assumed to be [property].

This result was first proved by [author] in [setting]. A similar statement appears in [reference], under the additional assumption that [assumption]. Our proof is closer in spirit to [reference]. In contrast with [reference], we do not assume [assumption]. The case [case] was treated independently by [author].

Suppose, to the contrary, that [assumption]. It suffices to show that [claim]. By [lemma], we may assume that [reduction]. We first treat the case [case], and then deduce the general case. This contradicts [fact], and the proof is complete. The converse follows by the same argument. Without loss of generality, we may assume that [condition].

The following example shows that the assumption [assumption] cannot be dropped. Note that [observation]. In general, [statement] fails, as the following example shows. The condition [condition] is satisfied, for instance, when [case].

We expect that [statement] holds in general, but we have not been able to prove it. It seems likely that [statement]. This suggests that [statement]. At present, we do not know whether [question]. Numerical evidence indicates that [observation].
It would be interesting to know whether [question]. A natural next step is to [direction]. We hope to return to this question in future work. We do not know whether the bound [bound] is sharp.
The author thanks [name] for helpful discussions. We are grateful to the referee for careful reading and valuable comments. This work was supported by [funder] under grant [number].

Unsupported claims. Writing "it is well known that" without a reference. Give the reference instead. False ease. Writing "obviously" or "clearly" when the step is not obvious to a reader. Explain the step or cite it. Inflated adjectives. Writing "very unique" or "very novel". These adjectives do not take degrees. Future tense for the paper. Writing "in this paper we will prove". Prefer "we prove". Indirect thanks. Writing "the author would like to thank". Prefer "the author thanks".
I use phrases as starting points and adapt them. Every "well known" fact has a reference. My comparisons with earlier work are precise and fair. My hedging matches the strength of my evidence.

d: How to prepare, submit and update a preprint on arXiv. Accounts and endorsement, choosing categories, licences, TeX source, versions, and the link with journal submission.
x: arXiv is the main preprint server for mathematics, physics, computer science and several neighbouring fields. Posting there makes your work visible immediately, establishes a public date, and lets readers find it before the journal version appears.

Check the journal policy. Almost all mathematics journals accept papers already posted on arXiv. Check the policy of your target journal anyway, especially in other fields. Agree with your co-authors. All authors must agree on the version, the title, the abstract and the timing. Polish the paper. The first version is the one most people will read. Do not post a rough draft.

You need an arXiv account. To submit to a category for the first time, you may need an endorsement: a confirmation from an established author in that category that you are part of the research community. arXiv has tightened this system over time, and an institutional email address on its own is no longer enough to be endorsed automatically in many cases. Read the current endorsement page on arXiv before your first submission. The usual route is to ask your supervisor or a co-author who already publishes in the category.

Choose one primary category, the one that best describes the paper. In mathematics, categories look like math.AG (algebraic geometry), math.NT (number theory), math.PR (probability). Add cross-lists only when the paper is genuinely relevant to another community. Too many cross-lists may be removed by moderators. Look at where similar papers are posted.

Submit the TeX source, not only a PDF. arXiv compiles it with its own TeX installation. Include all files needed: .tex, .bbl (the compiled bibliography), figures, custom style files. Remove unused files, comments you do not want public, and hidden notes. Comments in TeX source can be downloaded by anyone. Use standard packages. Compile locally with a clean, recent TeX distribution before uploading. Make figures in PDF or PNG for pdfLaTeX.

Title and abstract: the abstract field is plain text with limited TeX. Keep mathematics simple. Authors: in the order agreed by all authors. Comments field: number of pages and figures, and later the journal reference ("To appear in ..."). MSC classes for mathematics, and keywords.

arXiv asks you to choose a licence. The default arXiv licence gives arXiv the right to distribute the paper and leaves other rights to you. Creative Commons licences (such as CC BY) allow wider reuse. Some funders require a specific open licence. Check your funder's rules before choosing. A licence cannot be withdrawn once the paper is announced.

Submissions are checked by moderators and announced on a fixed daily schedule. A paper may be reclassified to another category or put on hold. Once announced, a paper cannot be removed. It can only be withdrawn, and the earlier versions stay visible.

Post a new version when you correct errors or when the journal version is accepted. Each version keeps its number (v1, v2, v3). Add a short note in the comments field explaining the change. After acceptance, update the journal reference and the DOI fields. Respect the journal's rules about posting the final accepted manuscript.

Add the arXiv number to your CV and web page. Send the link to researchers who will be interested, with a short personal note. Submit to the journal. Most journals let you submit directly from the arXiv identifier.

All co-authors approved the version and the timing. I have an endorsement for the primary category if needed. The TeX source compiles cleanly and contains no private comments. I chose the licence deliberately. I will update the journal reference after acceptance.

d: How to plan, build and deliver a research talk. Know the audience, follow the three-part structure, design clear slides or board work, rehearse, and handle questions.
x: A talk is not a paper read aloud. A good talk gives the audience one main idea, one main result, and the feeling that they understand why it matters. The details are in the paper.

Before writing anything, ask: who will be in the room? Departmental colloquium: researchers from all areas. Most of the talk must be accessible. Specialised seminar: people from your area. You can go further, but still start slowly. Conference talk: often 20 to 30 minutes. One result, one idea of proof. Job talk: a mix of general audience and experts. Show the big picture and your independence.

A classic rule divides the talk into three parts: For everyone (about a third). The context, the question, why it matters, an example everyone can follow. For the field (about a third). The precise statement of the results, how they compare with earlier work. For the experts (the rest). An idea of the proof, the main new ingredient. Every listener should leave with something. Most people will remember only the first part. Make it good.
Write down the one sentence you want people to remember. Then build the talk backwards: what does the audience need to know to understand that sentence? Remove everything else.

Board talks force a slower pace, which helps the audience follow. They are common in mathematics. Slides let you show pictures, diagrams and longer statements. Do not put too much on each slide. For slides: One idea per slide. Large font. Few words. No paragraphs. State theorems in a short, readable form. Hide technical conditions or move them to a remark. Use pictures and diagrams. Number slides so people can ask about a specific one. Plan about one slide per one to two minutes.

Rehearse aloud, standing, with a timer, at least twice. Give a practice talk to your group and ask for honest comments. Prepare a version that can be shortened by five minutes if the session runs late. Know which slides you can skip.

Speak slowly and look at the audience. Repeat the main question and the main result. Give examples before general statements. Finish on time. Running over is one of the few things audiences never forgive. End with a summary slide that stays on screen during questions.

Repeat the question so everyone can hear it. If you do not know the answer, say so and offer to discuss it afterwards. If a question is long or technical, suggest talking after the session. Thank people for their questions.

I know the audience and adapted the level. My talk has a part for everyone, a part for the field, a part for experts. I can state the main message in one sentence. I rehearsed aloud with a timer. I know which slides to skip if time is short.

d: How to search the literature systematically, organise what you read, and write a review that compares ideas instead of listing papers. Useful for a thesis chapter, a survey or the background section of a paper.
x: A literature review is not a list of summaries. It is an argument about the state of a field: what is known, how the results relate, and what is still open. Your reader should finish it with a map of the area.
Write one or two sentences that say what the review covers and what it does not. A clear scope keeps the search manageable and the text focused.

Start from two or three key papers and follow their references (backward search). Use citation databases to find who cites them (forward search): Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, zbMATH Open, MathSciNet if your library has access. Search arXiv listings in your categories for recent preprints. Read recent surveys and the introductions of recent theses. Record your search terms and sources, so you can repeat or extend the search.

Use a reference manager (Zotero, JabRef, or a plain BibTeX file) from the first day. For each paper, write a short note: main result, method, assumptions, relation to other papers. Use tags for themes, methods and open questions. Keep a table with one row per paper and columns for the dimensions you want to compare (setting, method, result, limitation).

Look at your table and notes. Group papers by: Theme: the different questions studied. Method: the different approaches to the same question. Chronology: when the history of an idea matters. Usually a review combines these. Choose the structure that best explains the field to a newcomer.

For each section, write about ideas, not papers. Compare: "Both [A] and [B] obtain [result], but [A] assumes [condition], while [B] uses [method]." "The approach of [A] was later simplified by [B]." "These results leave open the case [case]." Each paragraph should have a topic sentence that states a claim about the literature.
End each section, and the review as a whole, with what is unknown. These gaps motivate your own work. Be fair: a gap is not a criticism of earlier authors.

A list of papers with one paragraph each. Only recent papers, or only old ones. Misreporting results you did not read carefully. Check every claim against the source. Citing papers you did not read because other papers cite them.

My scope is written down in two sentences. I searched backward, forward and in recent preprints. I keep a comparison table and notes for each paper. My review is organised by ideas, not by papers. Each section ends with what is still open.

d: How to start and run a research collaboration, share work fairly, decide author order, and avoid the most common conflicts. Includes the conventions of mathematics and other fields.
x: Most research today is collaborative. Good collaborations produce better papers and lasting friendships. Bad ones produce delays and conflicts. A few habits make the difference.

Collaborations usually start from a conversation: after a talk, during a visit, at a workshop. To turn a conversation into a project: Write a short shared note after the discussion: the question, the idea, the first steps. Agree on a first concrete task for each person. Fix a date for the next meeting.

Shared files: use a shared repository (Git, Overleaf, or a shared folder) with a clear structure. One main .tex file, one bibliography. Regular meetings: short and frequent meetings keep a project alive. A weekly or fortnightly call is common. Written notes: after each meeting, write down what was decided and who does what. Honest communication: say when you are busy, when you are stuck, or when you think an idea does not work.

Being an author means taking responsibility for the content. All authors should: contribute substantially to the work, read and approve the final version, be able to explain and defend the main results.

Conventions differ by field. Know the convention of your field and discuss it early. Mathematics and theoretical computer science: authors are usually listed in alphabetical order of surname. This signals equal contribution. Changing the order is unusual and should be discussed explicitly. Experimental sciences: the first author did most of the work, the last author is often the group leader. Middle positions follow contribution. Some fields use contribution statements (such as the CRediT taxonomy) to describe each author's role. When collaborating across fields, agree on the convention at the start.
Common conflicts and how to avoid them

Unequal contribution: discuss roles openly. If someone stops contributing, talk before the paper is finished, not after. Different speeds: agree on deadlines and respect them, or renegotiate early. Credit for an idea: acknowledge people who contributed an idea but are not authors. Submission decisions: decide together which journal to target and when to post the preprint. Leaving a project: if you leave, say so clearly and agree on what happens to your contributions.

A PhD student should be an author on the papers that come from their thesis work. Discuss authorship with your supervisor early. In mathematics, a thesis is sometimes written alone even when the topic came from the supervisor. Practices vary: ask.
Thank people who helped: discussions, comments on drafts, corrections, hosting a visit. Ask them before thanking them by name for a specific idea.

We wrote a shared note at the start with the question and first tasks. We agreed on author order and the convention of our field. We have a shared repository and regular meetings. All authors approved the final version. People who helped are acknowledged.

d: How to choose conferences, apply for travel funding, prepare a short talk or poster, talk to senior researchers, and turn meetings into lasting professional relationships.
x: Conferences are where research communities meet. They are where you learn what people are working on now, where your future collaborators and letter writers first hear about you, and where many positions are discussed informally.

Large meetings (national society meetings, international congresses): broad, many parallel sessions, good for visibility. Specialised workshops: small, focused, often with more discussion time. Often the most useful for a PhD student. Summer schools: lectures for students and early-career researchers. Excellent to learn a topic and meet people of your generation. Research programmes at institutes (several weeks or months): ideal for intensive collaboration. Ask your supervisor which events matter in your area. Look at the websites of mathematical institutes and societies.

Many events offer travel grants for students and early-career researchers. Apply early and read the conditions. Your department, doctoral school or supervisor's grant may cover travel. National societies and some foundations have small travel grant programmes. Explain in your application why the event matters for your research.

Submit a short abstract: the question, the result, why it matters. A short talk (15–20 minutes) should present one result clearly. See Giving a research talk. A poster should be readable from two metres: a title, a picture, three or four boxes of short text.

Many students find this the hardest part. A few practical rules: Prepare: before the event, look at the list of participants and their recent papers. Choose a few people you want to talk to. Ask questions after talks: a good question is an easy way to start a conversation. Use breaks and meals: sit with people you do not know. Introduce yourself simply: your name, where you study, what you work on, in two sentences. Listen more than you speak: ask people what they are working on.
An elevator description of your work
Prepare three versions of what you work on: One sentence, for anyone. Thirty seconds, for a researcher in a neighbouring area. Two minutes, for a specialist.

Write down the names and topics of the people you met. Send a short email to the people with whom you had a real discussion: thank them, mention the topic, send a link to a relevant paper. Follow up on promises (sending a reference, a preprint, a question). Stay in touch: send your new preprints to the people who were interested.
A simple personal web page with your CV, papers and talks. An up-to-date profile on arXiv, ORCID and Google Scholar. Optional: a professional account where your community is active.

I chose events that match my research and stage. I applied for travel funding early. I prepared a one-sentence and a two-minute description of my work. I talked to at least three new people. I followed up by email within a week.

d: A year-by-year plan for the doctorate, how to work with your supervisor, keep a research journal, handle being stuck, protect your health, and finish on time.
x: A PhD is a long project with uncertain steps. You are learning to do independent research while producing results. Planning cannot remove the uncertainty, but it can make the path clearer.

Durations vary by country: about three years in France and the United Kingdom, three to four years in much of Europe, five to six in the United States and Canada (including coursework). Adapt the plan below to your programme. First phase: learn. Read the key papers and books of the area. Reproduce known proofs. Give a talk on a paper in the group seminar. Start a research journal. Second phase: first result. Work on a well-defined first problem with your supervisor. Write it up as a first paper or preprint, even if it is modest. Third phase: independence. Develop your own questions. Present at conferences. Start thinking about the thesis structure and postdoc applications. Final phase: finish. Write the thesis, apply for positions, prepare the defence.

Regular meetings: agree on a rhythm (weekly or fortnightly) and keep it, even when you have little progress. Saying "I am stuck on this lemma" is useful information. Prepare each meeting: a short list of what you did, what you are stuck on, and what you want to ask. Write notes after meetings: what was decided, what to read, what to try. Show written work early: a page of notes is easier to discuss than an idea in your head. Ask about expectations: how many papers before the defence, when to start writing, when to apply for postdocs.

Write every day, even a few lines: what you tried, what failed, what you read, what questions you have. The journal is your memory, your source of material for the thesis, and a record of progress on bad days.

Being stuck is the normal state of research. Some strategies: Work out more examples, especially small or degenerate cases. Weaken the question: prove a special case first. Strengthen the hypothesis: what extra assumption makes it work? Explain the problem aloud to someone else. Read a related paper with a fresh method. Change problems for a few days, then come back. Talk to your supervisor before weeks pass.

Protect a block of deep work every day, without email and messages. Write every day. Separate learning time, research time and writing time. Keep a simple list of tasks for the week. Say no to some extra commitments, especially in the final year.

A PhD can be isolating. Keep a life outside research: sport, friends, rest. Talk to other doctoral students. Most universities offer counselling services and doctoral schools have contacts for difficulties with supervision. Asking for help early is a sign of professionalism.
Teaching is valuable experience and often required for future positions. Keep it within the limits of your contract and plan your research time around it.

I have a rough plan for each phase of my PhD. I meet my supervisor regularly and prepare each meeting. I keep a research journal every day. I have strategies for when I am stuck. I protect time for deep work and for rest.

d: How to turn your papers and notes into a coherent thesis. Structure, the general introduction, chapters built from papers, writing schedule, working with the committee, and preparing the defence.
x: The thesis is the document that proves you can do independent research. It is also, for many readers, the most complete introduction to your topic. Plan it as a book, not as a collection of files.

Every university has rules: format, length, language, whether published papers can be included as chapters, deadlines for submission, composition of the committee. Read them at the start of your final year.

Monograph: a single unified text, organised by topic. Thesis by publication: a general introduction followed by your papers as chapters, sometimes with linking sections. Even in a thesis by publication, the general introduction is substantial work. It is the part that examiners and future readers read most closely.

The general introduction should: Present the field and the main questions for a non-specialist in your discipline. Explain the background needed to read the thesis. State your main results clearly, with their context. Explain how the chapters relate and in which order to read them. Mention open questions and future work. Many theses also include a summary in the national language of the university.

Unify notation across chapters, or explain the differences. Remove repetitions of the same background, or move shared background to a preliminary chapter. Add a short introduction to each chapter explaining its place in the thesis. State clearly which chapters come from joint work and what your contribution was.

Start early. Write the background chapter and parts of the introduction while you still do research. Plan backwards from the submission date. Leave time for your supervisor to read each chapter and for revisions. Write the introduction last, or rewrite it at the end, when you know exactly what the thesis contains. Fix a weekly target (pages or sections) and track it. A realistic plan for the final writing phase is several months, not weeks.

Use a standard thesis class or your university's template. Keep one bibliography file for the whole thesis. Use version control (Git) or regular backups in at least two places. Compile the full thesis regularly to catch errors early. Create an index of notation if your thesis uses many symbols.

Your supervisor usually proposes the reviewers. Send them a complete and polished version. Reviewers write reports, sometimes with corrections. Treat these like referee reports: correct what is wrong, clarify what is unclear, and keep a list of changes.

Prepare a talk adapted to the audience: committee, colleagues, sometimes family. Follow the three-part structure of Giving a research talk. Rehearse with your group. Prepare for questions on the whole thesis, the background, and future directions. After the defence, make any required corrections and submit the final version.

I know the rules of my university for format, length and deadlines. My general introduction presents the field, the results and the plan. Notation is consistent across chapters. I have a writing schedule with time for my supervisor's comments. My files are under version control with backups.

t: What a PhD expects from you
d: The unwritten rules of the doctorate. Own your project, bring questions rather than answers, ask whether a problem is worth solving, and make every expectation with your supervisor explicit.
x: Most new doctoral students arrive with the habits of a good student: solve the problem you are given, work harder when it does not work, and come back when you have the answer. These habits stop working in the first months of a PhD. Nobody tells you, because your supervisor has forgotten what the first year felt like and you do not yet know which questions to ask. This guide makes those unwritten expectations explicit.

Financially, a doctorate rarely pays off. In the United Kingdom, for example, the salary premium over a master's degree is small, and the years on a stipend are years of lower income. What justifies the years is what you become: an independent researcher who understands a problem better than anyone else. Treat the PhD as a project you run, not as a job someone supervises. You are not working for your supervisor. They designed the project and found the money. You choose how to explore it, which angle to take, and what you want to learn from it. Test whether you own it. If you can answer every question about your project, technical or general, it is yours. If you still need your supervisor to answer some of them, it is not yours yet. Present your own work. Give talks on it, at seminars and conferences. People quickly see who did the work by the answers to their questions.
What the supervisor does, and what you do

A supervisor provides the vision (where the project fits in the field, and why it matters), the resources, and the contacts with people who have the expertise you need. A supervisor also teaches, writes grants and runs several projects at once. Realistically, they can think about your project an hour or two each week. You can think about it every day. So the motivation has to come from you. If your project leaves you cold, try three things before giving up on it: Dig deeper. Find out why the question matters and to whom. Talk to people who care about it. Change the angle. Look for a method, an example or an application that interests you, inside the scope of the project. Treat it as training. Decide what skill you want to leave with: a technique, a computer tool, a way of writing. If nothing works after months, stopping is a legitimate and mature decision, not a failure.

The most common first-year mistake is to avoid your supervisor until you have results. At the edge of knowledge, being stuck is normal. You do not need results to book a meeting. A precise question, a failed attempt or a counterexample is enough. Agree on what meetings are for, and how often they happen. Start each meeting with the big picture, then go into detail only as far as needed. Your supervisor knows the field, not the details of your computations. If you wrote three pages to prepare, cut them to half a page.
Can do is not should do

In your studies, every exercise was worth solving because it counted for a grade. In research, you must decide what deserves your time. Before spending weeks on a proof, a computation or a program, ask: what will I learn, and does it move the project forward? A correct result can still be a waste of time. Most of your ideas will be weak. That is normal. Expose them early to people who will criticise them, and let the weak ones go quickly. This is how you build research taste.
Supervisors are busy. An unanswered email usually means it was forgotten, not ignored. Send reminders, more often than feels polite. A cancelled meeting is rarely personal.

Discuss authorship early. Do it before a collaboration starts, not when the paper is written. Conventions differ by field: in mathematics, authors are usually listed alphabetically. The guide on collaboration and authorship explains them. Reviews can be unfair. A harsh report is a judgment of one text by one person on one day. Separate the quality of your work from the tone of the report, keep what is useful, and move on.
Rest is part of the plan
There is always another deadline. If you do not schedule rest, you will not get it. After a submission or a missed deadline, take a day or two, then reflect on what went wrong and continue.

To work out for yourself: I know why I am working on my current problem. I have shown my latest idea to someone who could criticise it. I separate harsh feedback on my work from my worth as a researcher. I have scheduled rest in the coming weeks. To discuss with your supervisor: We agree on what meetings are for and how often they happen. I know what enough progress looks like before the next meeting. We have discussed authorship for every ongoing collaboration. I know the best way to follow up when an email gets no answer.

The PhD is a project you own, not a job you are given. Your supervisor brings vision and resources. You bring the drive. Bring questions to meetings, not only results. Ask whether a problem is worth solving before solving it. Make every expectation explicit, early.
This guide draws on two essays on Substack, which are worth reading in full: Patrik Reizinger, A PhD expectations guide, The Path to PhD, 2026. Davide Michieletto, How to win your PhD, 2026.

d: Research is a set of skills that can be trained. Choose your own problems, train your taste by making predictions, read beyond the trending papers, write everything down, shorten the loop between idea and test, and find people who tell you the truth.
x: Nobody teaches research directly. You receive a problem, a desk and the instruction to find something new. Most people then copy what they see from the outside: papers, talks, announcements. They learn to look like researchers. The actual work is a stack of smaller skills, and almost every one of them can be trained on purpose. This guide complements the research method with the habits that make that method work better year after year.

The physicist Richard Hamming liked to ask colleagues what the important problems of their field were, and then why they were not working on them. The question is uncomfortable because most of us do not choose our problems. We absorb them from a supervisor, a famous group or the paper everyone is discussing. An absorbed problem comes without its reasoning. You know that others find it important, but not why, and not what would make them drop it. On a fashionable problem you also compete with many people who started earlier. There are two ways to find a problem: Improve on the literature. Read papers and look for what can be generalised, sharpened or simplified. Start from what you want to exist. Choose a result or an understanding you genuinely want, and work backwards to the questions that lead there. Both are useful. The second is the more reliable source of original work, because it takes you where no survey goes.

Research taste is often described as a gift. It behaves more like a skill: it improves with predictions and corrections. Predict before you check. Before computing an example or running an experiment, write down what you expect. Compare afterwards. Guess the result from the method. Read the setup of a paper, hide the main theorem or the results section, and guess what it says. Forecast importance. Note which new papers you think will matter in two years. Check your list later. A few hundred predictions, each followed by a correction, change how you judge problems.

If you read only what everyone reads, you will have the same ideas as everyone, at the same time. Read older work. Many fields rediscover their own past. A classic paper or a twenty-year-old survey often contains ideas that were never fully exploited. Read outside your area. Methods travel between fields. A neighbouring subject is often where your next tool comes from. Read the paper, not the summary. The details, the remarks and the section on limitations are where the real information is.

The mathematician and engineer Claude Shannon recommended a simple move when stuck: shrink the problem until it becomes almost trivial, solve the small version, then add the difficulty back one piece at a time. In mathematics, this means the smallest dimension, the simplest example, the most degenerate case. The guide on managing your PhD lists more strategies for being stuck.

An idea feels complete until you try to write it. The page shows the assumption you never checked, the step that does not follow, the two claims that contradict each other. Keep a research log. For every attempt, write the hypothesis, what you did, what you expected, what happened, and what you now believe. Darwin wrote down every fact that contradicted his theory immediately, because he noticed that he forgot those facts first. Your memory does the same with failed attempts. Write some of it in public too: a clear expository note, a blog post, a talk. A clear explanation of a known result is a real contribution, and a body of clear writing shows how you think.

Research speed is mostly the speed at which you find out that you are wrong. Make every test cheap: Check an idea on the smallest example before attempting the general proof. Keep your computations, code and notes organised, so that redoing a calculation takes minutes, not a day. Try the rough version of every idea first. Let most of them fail early.

A general argument can hide a mistake that one explicit example reveals at once. Compute examples by hand. Read the output of your programs, not only the final number. When something fails, collect the failures, sort them, and attack the largest group first.

Hamming also observed that colleagues who worked with their office door closed got more done each year, but those who kept it open did the more important work, because interruptions told them what mattered. Keep your door open: answer emails, go to seminars, talk about half-finished ideas. Be generous. Share notes, code and corrections. Explain hard things simply. The returns come later and indirectly. A colleague who tells you an idea is bad before you spend three months on it is worth more than any tool.

I can say why my current problem is important, in my own words. I wrote down a prediction before my last computation or experiment. This month I read at least one older paper and one paper outside my area. My research log records failed attempts, not only successes. I tried the smallest case of my problem before the general one. I showed an unfinished idea to someone who could criticise it.

Choose problems for reasons you understand. Taste is trained by predictions and corrections. Read old work, other fields, and the papers themselves. Shrink the problem, test cheaply, and write everything down. Keep your door open and be generous.

This guide is built on the ideas of an essay on Substack, which collects many classic references: Vivek, how to be good at research, 2026. Richard Hamming, You and your research, talk at Bell Communications Research, 1986.

t: Skimming a paper in twenty minutes
d: You cannot read every paper in full. Read the few paragraphs that carry the story, then the figures and the topic sentences, and decide in twenty minutes whether a paper deserves a deep reading.
x: Thousands of papers appear every week. Experienced researchers do not read them from the first line to the last. They read a few places where the story is concentrated, decide quickly whether the paper matters to them, and keep the deep reading for the few that do. This guide gives a fast first filter. It comes before the three-pass method of How to read a research paper, which is for the papers you decide to keep.
Why a paper can be skimmed

A well-written paper has the shape of an hourglass. It starts broad, with the general question of the field, narrows to the precise question of the paper, stays narrow in the technical part, and widens again at the end to explain what the results mean. Because of this shape, a few paragraphs carry most of the story. The ecologist Brian McGill named five of them, the five pivotal paragraphs: The abstract: the whole story in compressed form. The first paragraph of the introduction: the broad question and the context. The last paragraph of the introduction: what the authors set out to do. The first paragraph of the discussion: the main findings, in plain words. The last paragraph of the discussion: what the findings mean for the field.

The ecologist Jonathan Tonkin builds a reading routine on these paragraphs. Here it is, with the times he suggests. Pass 1: title and abstract (2 minutes). What is the question, and why should I care? If you cannot say it in one sentence, stop. This pass works even on paywalled papers. Pass 2: objectives and figures (5 minutes). Read the last paragraph of the introduction, then the figures and their captions, without the text of the results. Do the figures support the story the authors announce? Pass 3: the remaining pivotal paragraphs (5 minutes). The first paragraph of the introduction, and the first and last paragraphs of the discussion. You now have the authors' version of the story. Remember that peer review does not guarantee that every claim is justified. Pass 4: topic sentences (8 minutes). Read the first sentence of every paragraph. In a well-written paper, these sentences alone reconstruct the argument. Pass 5: deep reading (as long as needed). Only if the paper deserves it. Go to the parts you need: the methods if you want to reproduce them, the proofs if you will use them, everything if you are refereeing. After pass four, most papers have given you what you need. Decide consciously whether to continue.

Mathematics papers rarely have a discussion section, but the hourglass is still there. The pivotal places are: The abstract. The first paragraph of the introduction: where the problem comes from. The statements of the main theorems, usually in the introduction, with the paragraph that follows each of them. The comparison with earlier work: what is new. The last part of the introduction or the final section: applications, examples and open questions. Replace the figures of pass two by the main theorems and one worked example. Replace the topic sentences of pass four by the statements of all the lemmas and propositions, read in order: they form the skeleton of the proof.

A new field. When you enter an unfamiliar area, read the whole introduction of several papers. It is the fastest way to learn the questions, the vocabulary and the main names. Surveys and very short papers. Their structure is different. Read the table of contents of a survey first, and read a short letter in full.

Search arXiv or the preprint server of your field. Check the authors' web pages and their university repositories. Use a tool such as Unpaywall, or the "all versions" link in Google Scholar. Write to the corresponding author. Most researchers are happy to send their paper.

After two minutes, I can state the question of the paper in one sentence. I read the objectives before the results. I checked that the figures or the main theorems support the announced story. I read the topic sentences before deciding to read in depth. I decided consciously whether this paper deserves a deep reading.

Most of a paper's story lives in five paragraphs. Skim in passes, each one longer than the last. Stop when you know enough. In mathematics, the main theorems and the comparison with earlier work play the role of the results and the discussion.
This guide is based on an essay on Substack, which builds on an earlier post by Brian McGill: Jonathan Tonkin, How I read a scientific paper in 20 minutes, Predirections, 2026.

d: What peer review is for, where it comes from, what it does well and what it does not. Knowing its limits helps you write papers that pass it, read reports calmly, and review fairly yourself.
x: Peer review is criticised from all sides. It is slow, decisions are partly random, and errors and fraud still get through. It is also how most scientific work is checked before it enters the record. You will spend your career on both sides of it, so it helps to know what it actually does. The practical side, from the cover letter to the answer to referees, is in the guide on submission and peer review.

The first scientific journal, the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, appeared in 1665. From early on, members of the Royal Society were asked to judge which submissions deserved publication. As research became more specialised, editors sent papers to experts. Systematic review before publication is much more recent. It spread between about 1950 and 1970, when public research funding grew very fast and the number of papers grew with it. Nature made external review a requirement only in 1973. Of Einstein's roughly three hundred papers, only one seems to have been sent to an external referee.

It improves the writing. Most changes requested by referees concern clarity and presentation. Surveys of authors and comparisons of preprints with published versions point in the same direction. It tempers claims. Referees ask authors to state limitations, to separate facts from speculation, and to quantify uncertainty. It guarantees readers. At least two experts read your paper carefully. For a young researcher without a network, this is valuable. It can reduce the weight of reputation. When reviewing is anonymous, a paper is judged more on its content and less on the name of its author or institution. It filters bold claims. Most spectacular claims turn out to be wrong. Experts are the best placed to notice it early, before a field spends years on them.
What peer review does not do

It is not a full verification. Referees rarely redo every experiment or every computation. In mathematics, a referee checks the main arguments, but responsibility for correctness stays with the authors. It is not reproducible. Studies of resubmitted papers show that two referees often disagree, and the same paper can be accepted or rejected depending on who reads it. It can discourage the unusual. Papers written to be "review-proof" tend to remove opinions, unfinished ideas and anything a referee could attack. It can reward hype. Authors overstate their results to pass the editor's first screening. This happens mostly at the desk-rejection step, before any referee reads the paper.
What this means for you as an author

Write for the editor first. The editor decides in minutes whether to send the paper out. State clearly and honestly what is new in the abstract and the introduction. Do not inflate. Treat rejection as noise and signal. Part of every decision is chance. Read the reports for what they reveal about your writing, revise, and submit elsewhere. Good work is almost always published in the end. Make the referee's work easy. Clear statements, complete proofs, explicit hypotheses, and a fair comparison with earlier work. Separate your worth from the report. A harsh report judges one text, on one day, by one reader.
What this means for you as a referee

Check what you can, and say what you did not. If you checked only the main proofs, write it. Judge the paper, not the author. Even when the review is not anonymous. Ask for clarity and honesty, not for the paper you would have written. Be open to the unusual, while asking for the evidence that a bold claim needs.

My abstract and introduction state what is new, without exaggeration. My limitations and open points are stated in the paper. I read referee reports for what they say about my writing, not about me. As a referee, I state which parts I checked in detail. As a referee, my requests concern correctness and clarity, not my own preferences.

Peer review in its modern form is only about seventy years old. It improves writing, tempers claims and gives every paper expert readers. It does not fully verify results, and its decisions are partly random. Write clearly and honestly for the editor and the referees, and do not take a decision personally.
This guide draws on an essay on Substack that defends peer review while taking its critics seriously: Dan Elton, A Defense of Peer Review, Asimov Press, 2024.

t: What older papers teach about writing
d: Papers written a century ago were often easier to read than today's. Keep the precision of modern writing, and take back what older papers did well. Say why you did the work, give one main idea, and state honestly what you do not know.
x: Open a paper from the 1920s and one from last year, in your own field. The old one is often easier to follow, even for a non-specialist. It says what problem the author was struggling with, why, and what was found. The recent one is usually more precise, more complete, and much harder to read. This guide explains how that happened and what you can take back from older papers without losing modern rigour.

The call for plain scientific prose is old. In 1667 Thomas Sprat, the first historian of the Royal Society, asked its members to reject ornament and write as briefly as possible. Darwin said much the same two centuries later. Yet for a long time, papers kept a personal voice: authors expressed doubt, enthusiasm and surprise. Several changes in the twentieth century made papers uniform: More papers. Public research funding grew enormously after the Second World War. Journals were flooded, and editors imposed tight formats such as the IMRAD structure (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion), which became almost universal in medical journals by the 1970s. Style manuals. Professional societies wrote rules for form and style. The first edition of the American Psychological Association's manual appeared in 1937, after years of debate in which some members warned that uniform pages would kill the life of science. Systematic peer review. Authors began to write papers that leave a referee nothing to attack: no opinions, no unfinished work, no admitted confusion. Citation metrics. Once citations and impact factors were counted, papers were also written to be cited, and many claims were packed into one paper. More authors per paper. A text written by a committee has less personal voice.

Clarity, precision and concision are real virtues. Standard structure and notation save the reader time. Jokes and ornament rarely help a reader who wants to understand a result. The aim is not to write like the seventeenth century, but to recover what made older papers readable.
What to take back from older papers

Say why you did the work. Older papers often began with the problem the author was struggling with. Your introduction should do the same: where the question comes from and why it matters. The guide on writing the introduction shows how. One main idea per paper. Many older papers contained one idea, stated clearly. A paper with ten claims of equal weight is hard to read and hard to remember. Put your main result first and organise the rest around it. State honestly what you do not know. Older authors wrote openly about doubts and open points. Separate clearly what you prove, what you conjecture and what you could not do. A remark or a final section on open questions is the natural place. Use an image when it helps. A well-chosen analogy or picture can make an idea understandable, and has led to discoveries: Kepler thought about planetary motion in terms of musical harmony. Use one when it clarifies, never as decoration. Write for a reader, not for the referee. Ask what a colleague in a neighbouring field needs to follow the paper, not only what a referee could object to. Short papers are allowed. A clear note with one good observation is a contribution.

Pick a classic paper of your field, written at least fifty years ago. Read its first page and the first page of a recent paper on a related topic. For each, write down in one sentence the problem, the main result and why it matters. Notice which one made this easy, and why. Then reread your own latest introduction with the same three questions.

My introduction says where the problem comes from and why it matters. My paper has one main result, stated first. Proved results, conjectures and open points are clearly separated. Every analogy or picture helps understanding. A colleague from a neighbouring field could follow my first page.

Modern scientific prose became uniform after the Second World War, through growth, style manuals, peer review and metrics. Keep its precision and its standard structure. Take back from older papers the motivation, the single main idea and the honesty about what is not known.

This guide draws on two essays on Substack: Roger's Bacon, Research Papers Used to Have Style. What Happened?, New Science, 2022. Jakob Schwichtenberg, How scientific writing lost its soul, 2025. For the other side of the debate, see the essay by Dan Elton cited in Understanding peer review, which argues that clarity and objectivity matter more than style.

d: Few doctoral graduates obtain a permanent academic position. Hiring committees decide on evidence, not potential. Know what evidence they look for, finish your projects, plan for the gaps in your record, and decide consciously whether to play.
x: Many students start a PhD hoping to become professors. Few know how small the chances are, or how the decisions are made. This guide describes the academic job market honestly, so that you can decide whether to aim for it and how. It complements the guides on postdoctoral applications and on managing your PhD.

Data are incomplete, and they vary by country and field. As an order of magnitude, for the United Kingdom: About one doctoral graduate in five enters a university research job, such as a postdoc, in the year and a half after the degree. Most of these contracts are fixed-term. Estimates suggest that only around one postdoc in ten eventually obtains a permanent academic position. Putting these together, very roughly, one student in a cohort of forty may end up in a permanent academic job. The odds improve in some fields and countries, and they are worse in others. Check the figures for your own field. Not every postdoc wants a permanent position either, and many careers outside academia use a doctorate well.

For most permanent research positions, a committee looks for evidence of three things: Research. You can publish excellent work, regularly. Funding. You can win grants, fellowships or other competitive money. Teaching. You can teach well. The weights differ between universities and countries, but for research positions the first two usually dominate, and the second depends heavily on the first. A grant panel is placing a bet. Publications show that you can turn an idea into a finished result that survives scrutiny. A committee cannot hire potential. It reads a CV and a few documents, among dozens or hundreds. Hard work, busy weeks and promising ideas are not visible there. Papers, grants and teaching experience are.

Many good researchers are excellent at starting projects and slow at finishing them. Academic careers reward completed stories: a question, a claim, the evidence, written up and submitted. At some point a collection of results must become a paper. If you have several open projects, the most useful step is often to close one of them, not to open another.

Identify the gap. Which of the three kinds of evidence is weakest in your record? Plan to fill it. Finishing a paper, writing a fellowship application, taking a course to teach, building a collaboration, or making your research identity clearer. Test, learn, adapt. Applications fail often. Each rejection tells you something about how you present your work. Rewrite, ask for feedback, apply again.

Supervisors and mentors can explain the rules, give feedback, write letters and create opportunities. They cannot become independent on your behalf. A letter that says you lead research is credible only if you did: you chose the question, made the claim, selected the evidence and drove the paper to the end. Practise this early. Bring your supervisor a proposed story for your next paper: the question, the main claim, the evidence, what is missing and why it matters. Then discuss it.
Luck, and what you can control

Luck matters: the right place, the right time, the right idea, the right opening. Opportunities are not distributed equally. But a lot of what looks like luck rests on years of work that nobody sees: skills, a network of people who trust your work, many applications written and rejected. That work does not guarantee anything. It changes the odds, and it lets you use an opportunity when one appears.

A rejected application is not a verdict on your worth as a scientist. It means that one committee, in one round, chose someone else. Keep the score of the game separate from your value as a person. You may also decide that the game is not worth playing: the uncertainty lasts too long, the sacrifices are too large, or the jobs incompatible with the life you want. That is a legitimate choice, not a defeat. Ask yourself early what you are willing to give for an academic career, and what you are not.

I know the realistic odds in my field and country. I know which of research, funding and teaching is weakest in my record. I have a plan to finish at least one open project this year. I have written, or started, a fellowship or grant application. I can present the story of my next paper myself. I have decided what I am willing, and not willing, to give for this career.

Permanent academic positions are rare, and decisions rest on visible evidence. Research, funding and teaching are the three kinds of evidence. Finish projects. Plan for the gaps in your record. Learn from rejections. Independence must be shown, not claimed. Deciding not to play is a legitimate choice.

This guide draws on an essay on Substack by a physicist who leads a research group, which gives the sources of the figures above: Davide Michieletto, Academia is a game. Learn the rules before you play, 2026.
